prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B035 first, and I agree that unanimity here reflects the science and not just convergence. The line from proglucagon processing, to the insulinotropic action of the truncated active peptide, to receptor biology, to drugs with large effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes is unusually complete. It is physiology that became medicine, with independent outcome trials and global use confirming it. It is also timely rather than premature. I would rather build the prize around the discovery of the hormone and its active form than around a single product.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited names cannot fit into three seats, and any trio omits someone decisive: Knudsen if we honour discovery, or one of the discovery figures if we honour development. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide is publicly contested, and the credited list leaves out Habener-type contributions. A prize that is seen as unfair on credit would damage an otherwise very strong case. The recognition also sits close to a pharmaceutical success story, which some will read as commercial more than scientific.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius opened with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the prize should span physiology to therapy and treating Mojsov's priority as credited but contested.
responses.response: I take the contestation seriously and I agree the physiology-to-therapy span is the right framing. But I still prefer Mojsov to Knudsen for this prize. The citation I propose is about the discovery of GLP-1 physiology and its active form, and Knudsen's analogue design is better described as drug development, which is real but belongs to a differently worded achievement. If the committee's evidence on Mojsov's priority turns out weak, I would move toward Knudsen as the third name rather than leave the translational leg empty. I do not think we should settle this on the strength of the opening ballots alone, since five of six of us chose Mojsov partly from recollection that has not been checked.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked the unfolded protein response (B047) second, as a conceptually original pathway with clear mechanism, while acknowledging that clinical translation is indirect and that choosing a basic cell-biology prize is partly a strategic question.
responses.response: I share the view that Walter and Mori are a clean, well-defined pair and that the mechanism is original. I ranked B047 fourth, not higher, because its medical consequence is still mostly conceptual, and I do not think a strong basic-biology discovery is made more urgent by being clean. I disagree that it should be paired with GLP-1 in a split prize, because that would force a reduction of the incretin credit to one or two names and make the harder attribution problem worse. I would keep B047 as a serious candidate for a later year rather than this one.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked imatinib and BCR-ABL inhibition (B011) second, as a coherent Lydon, Druker and Sawyers trio with a mature, well-confirmed targeted-therapy paradigm.
responses.response: I agree B011 is mature and that its clinical impact is unambiguous, and that is why it is not far from the top group for me, although I did not include it in my opening ranking. My hesitation is the one you flag: the upstream cytogenetic and oncogene discoveries (the Philadelphia chromosome and ABL work) make the scope of a citation contestable, and Novartis's role clouds individual credit. I think that this is a harder attribution problem than the one in B035, not an easier one, so I would not rank it above CAR-T on credit grounds.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked optogenetics (B039) second, as a transformative method for causal control of cells with a defensible Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel trio, while noting the six-name problem and limited medical relevance.
responses.response: Optogenetics is the candidate nearest to my own field, so I have tried to be strict. Its effect on experimental circuit neuroscience is real, and I ranked it fifth because the discovery is a tool and its credit is split across six people into at least two separate steps (channelrhodopsin function and neuronal deployment). A trio that leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck would be contested however it is drawn. I do not think that its clinical record is yet sufficient to place it above a therapy with proven benefit, and I would not support it for this year.

uncertainties: Which three of the four credited GLP-1 names best represent the discovery, and whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third seat, is unresolved and depends on priority evidence none of us has verified.
Whether the committee wants a physiology-led citation or one that also names the drug-development leg.
If B035 is awarded alone, the remaining question is whether a second, distinct achievement is possible within the three-person cap, which in practice it is not without cutting GLP-1 credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have a documented 2009 co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, but neither bears on any shortlisted ballot. My expertise in motor circuits touches B039 and B028 only indirectly, and I have weighed them on the common criteria.
